recipe.history:
Capers are the pickled or salt-cured flower buds of Capparis spinosa, a wild-growing plant native to the Mediterranean basin and parts of Asia that has thrived in rocky, arid terrain for thousands of years. The ancient Greeks and Romans prized them — Pliny the Elder wrote about them, they appear in texts from ancient Egypt and the Near East, and caper bushes grow wild from Morocco to Pakistan with almost aggressive indifference to poor soil. The Sicilians and the inhabitants of the island of Pantelleria off Tunisia cultivated the finest capers in the world, particularly the Pantelleria caper, which is salt-cured rather than brined and has a complexity and depth that the ubiquitous supermarket brine-packed version rarely approaches. The caper's flavor is produced by a compound called rutin, which breaks down during pickling into a distinctive mustard-like pungency — sharp, briny, floral, and slightly bitter all at once.

Capers came to American kitchens largely through the influence of Italian-American and Jewish-American cooking traditions in the early twentieth century. They were essential to chicken piccata, to smoked salmon and bagels, to the Sicilian caponata that Italian immigrants brought to New York, New Orleans, and San Francisco. Their role in burger culture developed later, in the wave of Mediterranean-influenced fast-casual cooking that swept American cities in the 2000s and 2010s. Chefs discovered that capers, chopped and folded into tartar sauce or aioli, or scattered whole and fried until crispy over a patty, provided a briny counterpoint to beef's richness that no other condiment could quite replicate. They punch above their weight — a single tablespoon can reorient an entire dish.

I went through a phase in my twenties when I put capers in everything. Pasta, salads, scrambled eggs, roasted vegetables. My then-roommate staged an intervention. He sat me down at the kitchen table with a jar of capers and said, very seriously, that I needed to consider the concept of restraint. I told him he simply didn't understand. Three weeks later I made a salad that was approximately forty percent capers and had to admit, privately and then publicly, that he had a point. The best application of capers I have ever found is fried: tossed in a dry skillet or in hot oil until they bloom open like tiny green flowers and turn golden and crispy, losing their brininess but gaining a nutty, salty crunch that is genuinely addictive on top of a burger.

Medium rare is the temperature at which a beef patty reaches its ideal state — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, where the fat has rendered just enough to flow freely through the muscle fibers, where the proteins have contracted enough to hold their shape but not so much that they've expelled all moisture. The fried capers in this recipe are crispy and salty, and they need the juiciness of a medium-rare patty beneath them — something that gives back when you bite in, that offers juice and richness to temper the capers' intensity. A well-done patty would turn this burger into a one-note salt bomb. Medium rare makes it a conversation.
ingredients: 2 tbsp capers, drained and finely chopped
60ml capers, drained and patted very dry
1 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly torn
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, butter, and herbes de Provence. Knead on medium 8 minutes until smooth and elastic. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 4 balls, proof on a parchment-lined sheet 45 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.

2. Make the caper-lemon aioli: Grate garlic cloves into a medium bowl. Add egg yolks, lemon juice, lemon zest, Dijon, and salt. Whisk vigorously. While whisking constantly, drizzle in the oil in a very slow, thin stream until fully emulsified and thick. Fold in the chopped capers. Taste and adjust lemon and salt. Refrigerate until needed.

3. Fry the capers: Pat the capers completely dry with paper towels — moisture will cause dangerous spattering. Heat olive oil in a small skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add capers in a single layer. Fry, stirring occasionally, 3 to 4 minutes until capers have opened like flowers and turned golden and crispy. Transfer to a paper-towel-lined plate. They will crisp further as they cool.

4. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Shape each into a patty 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.

5. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties 3 minutes undisturbed. Flip and lay a slice of provolone on each. Cook 2 to 2.5 minutes more until the internal temperature reaches 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). Remove and rest 3 minutes.
6. Toast bun cut sides in the skillet fat over medium heat until golden and crisp, about 90 seconds.

7. Assemble: Spread caper-lemon aioli generously on both bun halves. Place a leaf of butter lettuce on the bottom bun. Add the rested patty with melted provolone. Layer tomato slices and red onion rings on top. Scatter a generous pile of fried capers over everything. Finish with torn parsley and a pinch of flaky sea salt. Cap with the top bun. Serve with lemon wedges on the side.
